sections.title: Is there a subject?
sections.content: You know passive *se* and impersonal *se* from B1 Unit 6: with a noun the verb agrees with it, and with no noun the verb stays singular. The tricky cases are in between. When what follows is a particular person, Spanish adds the personal *a* (you know the personal *a* from A1 Unit 24). Then the person is an object, not a subject, so nothing can agree with it and the verb stays singular. The same happens when the noun comes after a preposition.

sections.title: Four patterns
rows: Houses are for sale. (a thing: the verb agrees)
People live well here. (no noun: singular)
They are looking for the people responsible. (person with a: singular)
People are talking about prices. (noun after a preposition: singular)

items.spanish: Se atendió a todos los clientes.
Se trabaja mucho en esta oficina.
items.english: People work a lot in this office.

sections.content: Compare *Se buscan empleados* (a general ad: staff wanted) with *Se busca a los empleados* (they are looking for particular employees). The *a* marks particular people as the object, and that is why the verb stays singular. A plural verb with *a* (*Se buscan a los responsables*) is a common mistake.
